pos: n. (proper name; chief of the house of Merari in the wilderness)
etymology: Hebrew Tsuri'el, my rock is God, from tsur, rock, and 'el, God.
biblical_def: Zuriel is the chief of the Levitical families of Merari at Sinai. “Of Merari was the family of the Mahlites, and the family of the Mushites: these are the families of Merari” (Numbers 3:33). “And the chief of the house of the father of the families of Merari was Zuriel the son of Abihail: these shall pitch on the side of the tabernacle northward” (Numbers 3:35). The Merarites carried the heaviest parts of the sanctuary: “the boards of the tabernacle, and the bars thereof, and the pillars thereof, and the sockets thereof” (Numbers 3:36), “And the pillars of the court round about, and their sockets, and their pins, and their cords” (Numbers 3:37). Zuriel led the men who bore the frame of God's dwelling through the wilderness. His name, my rock is God, suits the leader of those who carried the foundations and pillars. The sockets of the tabernacle were silver, cast from the ransom money of Israel; the house of God stood on redemption, and the Merarites under Zuriel carried it on their shoulders.

pos: n. (proper name; a Levite, son of Uzziel)
etymology: Hebrew Sithri, my hiding place or the LORD protects, from sether, a covert, a secret place.
biblical_def: Zithri is a Levite of the house of Kohath, the youngest named son of Uzziel. “And the sons of Kohath; Amram, and Izhar, and Hebron, and Uzziel” (Exodus 6:18). “And the sons of Uzziel; Mishael, and Elzaphan, and Zithri” (Exodus 6:22). He was a cousin of Moses and Aaron. His brothers were the men called when Nadab and Abihu died before the LORD for offering strange fire: “And Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel the uncle of Aaron, and said unto them, Come near, carry your brethren from before the sanctuary out of the camp” (Leviticus 10:4). Zithri is not named in that grim task, but he belonged to the family that learned at close hand that God will be sanctified in them that come near Him. His name is the word for a covert, the secret place of the Most High. The Levite whose name meant hiding place served a God who is both a refuge to the humble and a consuming fire to the presumptuous.

pos: n. (proper name; a doorkeeper for the ark under David)
etymology: Hebrew Yechiyah, the LORD lives, from chayah, to live, and Yah.
biblical_def: Jehiah is one of the doorkeepers appointed when David brought the ark to Jerusalem. “And Berechiah and Elkanah were doorkeepers for the ark” (1 Chronicles 15:23). “And Shebaniah, and Jehoshaphat, and Nethaneel, and Amasai, and Zechariah, and Benaiah, and Eliezer, the priests, did blow with the trumpets before the ark of God: and Obededom and Jehiah were doorkeepers for the ark” (1 Chronicles 15:24). David had learned through Uzza's death that the ark must be carried as God commanded, by Levites, and he now ordered the procession with priests, singers and porters. “So David, and the elders of Israel, and the captains over thousands, went to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of the house of Obededom with joy” (1 Chronicles 15:25). “Thus all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the LORD with shouting” (1 Chronicles 15:28). Jehiah's place was the door. His name means the LORD lives, and he guarded the throne of the living God among His people.

pos: n. (proper name; son of Tikvah, in the matter of the strange wives)
etymology: Hebrew Yachzeyah, the LORD sees, from chazah, to see, to behold, and Yah.
biblical_def: Jahaziah the son of Tikvah is named in Ezra's account of the reform of the mixed marriages. Ezra had said, “Ye have transgressed, and have taken strange wives, to increase the trespass of Israel” (Ezra 10:10). The people proposed that the matter be handled by appointed times and judges, “until the fierce wrath of our God for this matter be turned from us” (Ezra 10:14). Then: “Only Jonathan the son of Asahel and Jahaziah the son of Tikvah were employed about this matter: and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite helped them” (Ezra 10:15). The margin gives the Hebrew as “stood,” and the phrase can mean they stood over the matter or stood against the proposal; the Authorized Version takes it as their appointment to the work. Either way, the work went forward: “And the children of the captivity did so” (Ezra 10:16). Jahaziah's name means the LORD sees. Nothing hidden in the households of Judah was hidden from God, and the reform brought it into the light.

corruption_paragraphs: Modern readers often call Ezra 10 harsh, as if the separation from foreign wives were ethnic exclusion. The issue was idolatry, not race: the wives were of the peoples of the land whose abominations had brought the exile. The same law that forbade these marriages welcomed Ruth, who took the God of Israel for her God.

The New Testament keeps the principle in its own form. Believers are to marry “only in the Lord,” and a believer already married to an unbeliever is not to depart (1 Corinthians 7:12–13, 39). Ezra's reform was a covenant renewal in a crisis of apostasy, not a pattern for dissolving Christian marriages.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Parosh who put away a strange wife)
etymology: Hebrew Yizziyah, the LORD sprinkles or the LORD unites; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Jeziah is one of the sons of Parosh who had taken a foreign wife and put her away in Ezra's reform. “Moreover of Israel: of the sons of Parosh; Ramiah, and Jeziah, and Malchiah, and Miamin, and Eleazar, and Malchijah, and Benaiah” (Ezra 10:25). The scene began in the rain: “all the people sat in the street of the house of God, trembling because of this matter, and for the great rain” (Ezra 10:9). Those found guilty “gave their hands that they would put away their wives; and being guilty, they offered a ram of the flock for their trespass” (Ezra 10:19). The record ends soberly: “All these had taken strange wives: and some of them had wives by whom they had children” (Ezra 10:44). Parosh was the largest family of the first return, and seven of its sons are named. Jeziah's name is preserved in a list of sinners who repented at cost. The Spirit recorded the names not to shame them forever but to show that the people turned.

etymology: Hebrew Yishshiyah, the LORD lends or whom the LORD forgets not; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Ishijah is one of the sons of Harim named among those who had married foreign wives. “And of the sons of Harim; Eliezer, Ishijah, Malchiah, Shemaiah, Shimeon” (Ezra 10:31). The reform began with a confession from the people themselves: “And Shechaniah the son of Jehiel, one of the sons of Elam, answered and said unto Ezra, We have trespassed against our God, and have taken strange wives of the people of the land: yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing” (Ezra 10:2). “Now therefore let us make a covenant with our God to put away all the wives” (Ezra 10:3). Ezra called them to “make confession unto the LORD God of your fathers, and do his pleasure” (Ezra 10:11). Ishijah was a son of a priestly family, Harim having been one of the courses of priests. His name stands in the list of those who obeyed the call. There was hope in Israel concerning this thing, because there is forgiveness with God for those who confess and forsake their sin.

pos: n. (proper name; a chief priest who returned with Zerubbabel)
etymology: Hebrew Ma'adyah, ornament of the LORD or the LORD's delight; spelled Moadiah in Nehemiah 12:17.
biblical_def: Maadiah is one of the chief priests who came up from Babylon with Zerubbabel. “Now these are the priests and the Levites that went up with Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra” (Nehemiah 12:1). The list continues: “Miamin, Maadiah, Bilgah” (Nehemiah 12:5), and closes, “These were the chief of the priests and of their brethren in the days of Jeshua” (Nehemiah 12:7). A generation later his house was headed by Piltai: “of Moadiah, Piltai” (Nehemiah 12:17), with the spelling slightly changed. Maadiah's name may mean ornament of the LORD. He was among the first priests to return to a ruined city and an empty altar, and his family continued in the service into the days of the high priest Joiakim. The altar was rebuilt before the walls, and the priests who came first kept the worship of God alive among a small and struggling people.

etymology: Hebrew Merayah, rebellion or the LORD's contention; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Meraiah is the head of the priestly house of Seraiah in the days of the high priest Joiakim. “And in the days of Joiakim were priests, the chief of the fathers: of Seraiah, Meraiah; of Jeremiah, Hananiah” (Nehemiah 12:12). Seraiah's house was the first named among the priests who returned with Zerubbabel: “Now these are the priests and the Levites that went up with Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra” (Nehemiah 12:1). Meraiah led it in the next generation. The list belongs to the age of reform: “These were in the days of Joiakim the son of Jeshua, the son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor, and of Ezra the priest, the scribe” (Nehemiah 12:26). The meaning of Meraiah's name is uncertain. His place in the record shows the priesthood handed on from father to son, as the law required, in the years when the walls were built and the law was read again.

pos: n. (proper name; one of David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew Mibchar, choice, the choicest, from bachar, to choose.
biblical_def: Mibhar the son of Haggeri is one of David's mighty men in Chronicles. “Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibhar the son of Haggeri” (1 Chronicles 11:38). The margin reads “the Haggerite.” The parallel list in Samuel reads at this point, “Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite” (2 Samuel 23:36), so that the two lists name the same pair of warriors in differing forms. The roster belongs to “the chief of the mighty men whom David had, who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom” (1 Chronicles 11:10), and to “the valiant men of the armies” (1 Chronicles 11:26). Mibhar's name means choice, a fitting word for the men chosen out of all Israel for the king's company. Their names are kept as a picture of the chosen men of a greater King, who are called and chosen and faithful.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of king Jeconiah)
etymology: Hebrew Malkiram, my king is exalted, from melek, king, and rum, to be high.
biblical_def: Malchiram is a son of Jeconiah, the king of Judah carried captive to Babylon. “And the sons of Jeconiah; Assir, Salathiel his son” (1 Chronicles 3:17), “Malchiram also, and Pedaiah, and Shenazar, Jecamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah” (1 Chronicles 3:18). Jeremiah had pronounced a curse on Jeconiah: “Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper in his days: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David” (Jeremiah 22:30). Jeconiah had sons, Malchiram among them, but none of them reigned. The royal line ran on through Salathiel and Pedaiah to Zerubbabel, who governed but never sat as king. Matthew traces the legal line of Joseph through this house: “Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel” (Matthew 1:12). Malchiram's name says my king is exalted, yet he was born a prince in exile without a throne. The true King of that line would be exalted, not by Jeconiah's seed after the flesh, but by the virgin birth of the Son of David.

corruption_summary: The curse on Jeconiah is called a contradiction of the promise to David; Christ's virgin birth answers both.
corruption_paragraphs: Skeptics set Jeremiah's curse on Jeconiah's seed against the promise of an eternal throne to David's house. Matthew shows Joseph's legal descent through Jeconiah, and Luke shows Mary's through Nathan. Christ, born of the virgin, inherits the legal right through Joseph without being Jeconiah's seed after the flesh.
This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps both His curses and His promises, and Christ fulfils them together.
